chapters.s: Keshava’s later life moves the philosophical cycle into Garh Narikel. The water clock becomes an image of disciplined speech and delayed hearing, while an unfinished case teaches Budhua that a witness must preserve another person’s words rather than complete them on the person’s behalf.

chapters.t: The Light of the Leatherworkers' Quarter
chapters.s: It concerns the leatherworkers’ quarter of Garh Narikel—which will be mentioned again much later in Water-Burial Among the Crocodiles—and that part of Gangesha Upadhyaya’s life which remained hidden behind the brilliance of the shastras. Having said this, Sutradhara remained silent for a while, then joined his palms and bowed to the assembly.

Budhua, who has carried the arguments and memories of the preceding chapters, enters the water among the crocodiles and dies. From that water-burial the long-lived Budhba ghost is born, transforming a mortal witness into the figure who will guard names across the centuries.

Exactly one year after Budhua’s water-burial—the first test of the Budhba ghost. From this night begin both the story of Garh Narikel’s embankment and the seed of the belief that “a human witness is half a ghost.” The Kosi, Kamala, and Balan river regions of Mithila have historically been prone to flooding, and the traditional allocation of resources for building and maintaining embankments has often reflected social hierarchy…

Twenty years after the flood. Gauri, who as a child had heard Budhba’s voice, is now the village’s principal healer—and for that very reason becomes the centre of a conspiracy. In many regions of India, especially among Adivasi and other marginalised communities, accusations of “witchcraft” have historically often been connected with land disputes, family enmity…

The torch-bearing crowd has reached the gate of the leatherworkers’ quarter—and the village women have now changed their decision to remain silent. That night, after seeing the torches at the gate, the awakened quarter sang a song—
chapters.g: In Chapter -87, the collective testimony of the village women rises beyond individual fear into a collective truth. It offers a communal, folk-based form of the theory of verbal testimony (shabda-pramana) attributed to Vachaspati Mishra in Chapter -96—the speaker’s intention, the hearer’s trust, and the truthfulness of the moment.…

chapters.s: After Yashpati leaves the village for the royal court at Darbhanga, Budhba sees for the first time something he cannot place within any boundary of the world he understands—as though time itself were a crocodile that devours ages, but not names. That day, remembering the generations that had passed, Budhba sang a folk refrain—
chapters.g: Chapter -86 deliberately breaks the simple, one-directional flow of chronology, in the same way that in Part 1, during the kabaddi game in Channa Grove, “ghosts can cross 1885, 1934, 1977, and the present in a single turn.” This technique—sometimes called “magical realism” or postmodern chronological rupture in literary criticism—is not merely a stylistic experiment here.…

chapters.s: Yashpati has not returned empty-handed from the royal court at Darbhanga: this time it is not merely the leatherworkers' quarter and Gauri that are in his sights, but the pipal Witness Tree itself. That day, on hearing the Amil's order, the villagers sang a proverb-song—
chapters.g: In both medieval and modern periods, outside authorities have at times destroyed the local, autonomous traditions of marginalised communities—religious or medicinal—in the name of “eradicating superstition,” while overlooking the social functions embedded in those traditions: communal memory, justice, or health care. Chapter -85 deliberately refuses a simple answer to this conflict.…

chapters.s: The men of the village have gone into the forest in search of Yashpati—but what they find there leaves more questions than answers. That day, listening to the silence of the forest, Budhba sang a proverb-song—
chapters.g: Chapter -84 deliberately refuses to make Yashpati's fate completely clear: he is shown neither dead nor alive. This uncertainty is not accidental. Throughout Water-Burial Among the Crocodiles, Budhba's power as a witness, however far-reaching, is never complete; there is always some angle he cannot see. That limit gives the story a realistic foundation: no witness, however powerful, can be omniscient.…

chapters.s: One month after Yashpati’s disappearance, the village livestock begins to vanish mysteriously—and Budhba, trying to understand the limits of his own power, goes beyond the village to the one person who may carry an older memory even than his. That day, casting her net at the river ghat, Sonama Majhin sang—
chapters.g: Chapter -83 deliberately brings a third tradition of memory into the story: Sonama Majhin’s fisherfolk, water-based folk tradition. It belongs neither to the Brahmanical classical tradition of Vachaspati, Udayana, and Gangesha, nor to the leatherworkers’ quarter and its herbal tradition.…
